title: 22. Interview: Cassandra
summary: Interview Q&A for Cassandra — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Cassandra interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Why is Cassandra called "masterless" and what does that buy you?
**Answer:** Cassandra has no primary, no leader, no coordinator election — every node is equal and can serve any client request. The first node a client contacts becomes the **coordinator** for that request; the coordinator hashes the partition key, finds the replicas, and forwards. If the coordinator itself dies, the client just connects to a different node. This buys you three things: **(1) No failover downtime** — losing any node (or even a whole AZ) doesn't impact availability; the cluster just routes around it. Compare to MongoDB replica sets, which lose writes for ~10 seconds during a primary election. **(2) Linear horizontal scaling** — add a node, it bootstraps (joins the ring, takes token ranges, streams data from neighbors), and immediately shares load. There's no "leader bottleneck" coordinating writes. **(3) Multi-DC active-active** — clients in each DC write to local nodes; Cassandra replicates across DCs asynchronously. Each DC is fully writable. The trade-off: no leader means **no global ordering** — Cassandra is AP in CAP, so under network partitions it stays available but may serve stale data. Also, the masterless design means every node must know about every other (gossip membership), which limits cluster size to ~1000 nodes per DC in practice. Real-world: Apple's 75k-node iMessage cluster is split into many smaller rings, each fully masterless.
**Visual:**
```
Masterless (Cassandra):
  Client -> any node (coordinator)
            |
            v
  +---+ +---+ +---+ +---+ +---+ +---+
  |N1 | |N2 | |N3 | |N4 | |N5 | |N6 |   <- all equal
  +---+ +---+ +---+ +---+ +---+ +---+
            |
            +-> hashes key, finds replicas N3,N4,N5
            +-> forwards to N3,N4,N5 in parallel
            +-> acks when CL (e.g., QUORUM=2) reached

  N2 dies?  Client just connects to N1 (or any other).
            No election, no downtime.

Master-slave (MongoDB replica set):
  Client -> Primary (only)
            |
            v
            Primary dies -> 10s election -> new primary
            During election: writes fail.
```

### Q2. What is the difference between partition key, clustering key, and primary key in Cassandra?
**Answer:** The **primary key** in Cassandra is the combination of **partition key + clustering key** (and optionally static columns). The **partition key** is the first part of the primary key — it determines which node(s) own the row via Murmur3 hashing. All rows with the same partition key live on the same set of replicas (the partition). The **clustering key** is the rest of the primary key — it determines the sort order of rows *within* a partition. For example, `PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), created_at, post_id)` means: partition by `user_id` (rows for the same user live together on the same nodes), and within each user's partition, rows are sorted by `created_at` then `post_id`. This enables efficient queries like `WHERE user_id = 'alice' AND created_at > '2024-01-01' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50` — a single-partition range scan that returns in single-digit milliseconds. **Critical rule**: a `WHERE` clause must include the full partition key (Cassandra can't query across partitions efficiently without `ALLOW FILTERING`, which is slow). You can filter on clustering key ranges *within* a partition. This is why Cassandra modeling is **query-driven** — you design tables around the queries you'll run, often duplicating data into multiple tables to support different access patterns. Real-world: Instagram's feed table is `PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), created_at)` so "give me Alice's latest 50 posts" is a fast single-partition scan.
**Visual:**
```
CREATE TABLE posts (
  user_id    text,
  created_at timestamp,
  post_id    uuid,
  content    text,
  PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), created_at, post_id)
);

  Partition key:    user_id          (determines which node)
  Clustering key:   created_at, post_id (sort within partition)
  Primary key:      user_id, created_at, post_id (full)

Partition for user_id='alice':
  +---------------------------------------+
  | alice | 2024-10-01 10:00 | p1 | "hi"  |
  | alice | 2024-10-01 11:00 | p2 | "yo"  |   <- sorted by created_at
  | alice | 2024-10-02 09:00 | p3 | "..." |
  +---------------------------------------+
  All on the same replicas (hash('alice') -> ring range)

Query: SELECT * FROM posts
       WHERE user_id='alice'
         AND created_at > '2024-10-01'
       ORDER BY created_at DESC
       LIMIT 50;
  -> single-partition scan, sub-10ms
```

### Q3. What is tunable consistency and how do you choose a consistency level?
**Answer:** Every Cassandra read/write specifies a **consistency level** (CL) — how many replicas must respond before the operation is considered successful. Levels: `ONE` (1 replica, fastest), `TWO`, `THREE`, `QUORUM` (floor(N/2)+1), `LOCAL_QUORUM` (quorum in local DC only), `EACH_QUORUM` (quorum in every DC, slowest), `ALL` (all replicas, fails if any down), `LOCAL_ONE`, `SERIAL`/`LOCAL_SERIAL` (for lightweight transactions using Paxos). The strong-consistency formula: **R + W > N** guarantees reads see the latest write (where N = replication factor). For RF=3: QUORUM reads (R=2) + QUORUM writes (W=2) → R+W=4 > 3 → strong. ONE + ONE → R+W=2 < 3 → eventually consistent (may read stale data right after write). Choose based on workload: **Financial / user-data writes** → `LOCAL_QUORUM` (survives a node failure, no cross-DC latency). **Cache-like reads** → `LOCAL_ONE` (fast, stale is OK). **Critical reads after writes** → `QUORUM` reads + `QUORUM` writes (linearizable). **Multi-DC strong consistency** → `EACH_QUORUM` (slowest, accepts no stale data even cross-DC). The trade-off: stronger CL = more replicas contacted = higher latency. `LOCAL_ONE` reads return in ~2-5 ms; `QUORUM` reads in ~10-20 ms (waits for the slowest of 2 replicas). Real-world: Netflix uses `LOCAL_QUORUM` for writes (must survive node failure locally) and `LOCAL_ONE` for most reads (acceptable to read 1-2 seconds stale); they accept that cross-DC failover might lose the last few seconds of writes — a deliberate trade-off for low latency.
**Visual:**
```
RF=3 cluster. CL options:

  CL          Replicas waited   Failure tolerance   Latency
  ----        ----------------   -----------------   -------
  ONE         1 of 3            loses 2 nodes OK    ~3 ms
  QUORUM      2 of 3            loses 1 node OK     ~10 ms
  ALL         3 of 3            loses 0 nodes       ~20 ms
  LOCAL_ONE   1 in local DC     DC-aware, fast      ~3 ms
  LOCAL_QUORUM 2 in local DC    DC-aware, durable    ~10 ms
  EACH_QUORUM quorum in EACH DC slowest              ~50+ ms

Strong consistency formula: R + W > N

  RF=3, R=QUORUM(2), W=QUORUM(2):  2+2=4 > 3 -> STRONG
  RF=3, R=ONE(1),    W=ONE(1):    1+1=2 < 3 -> eventual
  RF=3, R=ONE(1),    W=QUORUM(2): 1+2=3 = 3 -> "read-your-writes"
                                     (mostly OK, edge cases stale)

Pick by workload:
  - user profile (write-once, read-many): W=LOCAL_Q, R=ONE
  - counters / inventory:                 W=QUORUM,  R=QUORUM
  - cache / precomputed:                  W=ONE,     R=ONE
```

### Q4. How does Cassandra's gossip protocol work, and why is phi accrual detection better than a fixed timeout?
**Answer:** Every second, each Cassandra node picks 1-3 random peers and sends them its view of the cluster (which nodes are alive, their token ranges, schema versions, rack/DC). The recipient merges this with its own view and gossips the merged state forward. Within O(log N) seconds, the entire cluster converges on a consistent view — even for 1000-node clusters, convergence is under 30 seconds. **Phi accrual failure detection** improves on fixed timeouts by tracking the **inter-arrival time** of gossip from each peer (normally ~1 second). If a peer's gossip arrivals stop, the suspicion level `phi` rises continuously based on the deviation from the normal distribution. When `phi` exceeds a threshold (default 8), the peer is marked DOWN. This is better than fixed timeouts because: **(1) Adapts to network conditions** — a slow link raises the baseline inter-arrival time, so phi doesn't false-positive on a temporarily slow peer. **(2) Continuous value** — operators can see "phi=4.2 (suspicious but not down)" rather than a binary alive/dead. **(3) No magic numbers** — `phi=8` mathematically means "the probability of this peer being alive given the observed arrivals is < 0.0001." Real-world: Netflix's Chaos Monkey kills nodes randomly in production; phi detection catches the failure in ~10 seconds and the cluster routes around it without false-positives during normal network jitter. The trade-off: 10-second detection latency is too slow for some workloads; you can lower the threshold to phi=5 for faster detection at the cost of more false-positives.
**Visual:**
```
Gossip (every 1 second):

  N1 picks 2 random peers (say N3 and N5)
    sends: "I'm alive, my tokens, schema ver, DC, rack,
            here's what I think of others: [N2 up, N4 down, ...]"
    N3 replies: "thanks, here's my view: [N2 up, N6 up, ...]"
    N1 merges: takes latest timestamps of each piece of state
    N1 gossips the merged state to N5 next round

  Within ~log2(N) seconds, all nodes share the same view.

Phi accrual detection (for N4):

  Normal: gossip from N4 every 1s (mean=1s, sigma=0.2s)
  T=0  N4 last seen
  T=1  no gossip from N4 (phi=0.5, normal jitter)
  T=2  no gossip (phi=1.8, suspicious)
  T=5  no gossip (phi=4.2, very suspicious)
  T=10 no gossip (phi=8.0 -> mark N4 DOWN)

  Adaptivity:
    if network is normally jittery (sigma=1s),
    phi rises slower -> fewer false positives
    if network is normally stable (sigma=0.05s),
    phi rises faster -> quicker detection
```

### Q5. Why does Cassandra use an LSM tree instead of a B-tree?
**Answer:** A **B-tree** (used by PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB) does in-place updates — to change a row, the engine reads the disk page, modifies it, writes it back. This causes **write amplification** (one logical write may rewrite 4-16 KB of disk) and **random I/O** (each update seeks to a different disk location). Under heavy write load, B-trees become disk-seek-bound. An **LSM tree** (Log-Structured Merge tree, used by Cassandra, RocksDB, HBase) does **append-only writes** — every write goes to (a) an append-only commit log (sequential I/O) and (b) an in-memory memtable (no disk I/O at all). The write acks immediately without seeking. When the memtable fills, it's flushed to disk as an immutable SSTable (sequential I/O). The trade-off: **reads are slower** — to read a key, you check the memtable, then potentially many SSTables (using Bloom filters to skip irrelevant ones), merging the results. **Compaction** (background merging of SSTables) controls read amplification. For write-heavy workloads (Cassandra's sweet spot — IoT events, time-series, user activity logs), the LSM trade-off is a clear win: writes are 5-20× faster than B-trees because there's no seek and no write amplification. For read-heavy workloads with random updates, B-trees usually win. Real-world: Cassandra handles 1M+ writes/sec per cluster on commodity hardware; the same hardware running PostgreSQL would do ~50k writes/sec. The downside: Cassandra reads need 3+ disk I/Os in the worst case (memtable miss + multiple SSTables), which is why read-heavy analytical workloads often use other systems.
**Visual:**
```
B-tree (PostgreSQL):
  UPDATE row X
    1. find page containing X (random read)
    2. read page into buffer
    3. modify in place
    4. write page back (random write, 4-16KB)
    5. fsync WAL
  Write amplification: ~10x (full page write per row change)
  Disk pattern: random I/O (seek-bound)

LSM tree (Cassandra):
  INSERT row X
    1. append to commit log (sequential write, fsync)
    2. insert into memtable (in-memory, no disk)
    3. ack client
  Write amplification: ~1x (compaction may rewrite later)
  Disk pattern: sequential I/O (throughput-bound)

  Memtable flush (when full):
    sort memtable -> write SSTable-001 (sequential)

Read X:
    1. check memtable (in-memory)
    2. check Bloom filter for each SSTable
    3. read from matching SSTables (random read each)
    4. merge by timestamp, return latest
  Read amplification: 1 to N disk I/Os (B-tree = 2-4)

Trade-off:
  Writes:  LSM 5-20x faster than B-tree
  Reads:   B-tree 2-5x faster than LSM
  Best for LSM: write-heavy, time-series, append-mostly
  Best for B-tree: read-heavy, frequently updated, ad-hoc queries
```

### Q6. What are the three compaction strategies and when do you use each?
**Answer:** Cassandra offers three compaction strategies: **(1) Size-Tiered Compaction (STCS)** — merges similarly-sized SSTables into a bigger one when there are `min_threshold` (default 4) of them. Best for **write-heavy workloads** (low write amplification) but reads may touch many SSTables (high read amplification). Use for: time-series where you read mostly recent data; write-heavy workloads with infrequent reads. **(2) Leveled Compaction (LCS)** — organizes SSTables into levels (L0, L1, L2...) where each level is 10× the size of the previous; each level has non-overlapping SSTables. A read touches at most one SSTable per level (so ~4-5 total instead of 20+). Best for **read-heavy workloads** (low read amplification) but writes are amplified ~10× as they propagate through levels. Use for: read-heavy customer-profile lookups, message inbox reads. **(3) Time-Window Compaction (TWCS)** — groups SSTables by time window (e.g., 1 day) and compacts within each window independently. When a window expires (TTL), the whole SSTable is dropped — no tombstones, no compaction overhead. Best for **time-series with TTL** (metrics, logs, sensor data). Use for: IoT metrics with 30-day retention, application logs with 7-day retention. Real-world: Netflix's viewing history uses TWCS with 1-day windows and 90-day TTL — old data is dropped instantly by file deletion, not by tombstone compaction. The default in modern Cassandra is STCS; switch to TWCS for time-series, LCS for read-heavy profiles. Wrong strategy = slow reads (STCS for read-heavy) or slow writes (LCS for write-heavy).
**Visual:**
```
Size-Tiered (STCS):
  SSTables: [S1][S2][S3][S4]  -> merge -> [S_big1]
  Pros: low write amplification (each write rewritten ~2-3x)
  Cons: many SSTables -> reads touch 5-20 of them
  Use: write-heavy, time-series (mostly recent reads)

Leveled (LCS):
  L0: [S1][S2][S3]      (overlapping, from memtable flushes)
  L1: [S4]              (10x size of L0, non-overlapping)
  L2: [S5]              (10x size of L1)
  ...
  Pros: read touches <= 1 SSTable per level (~4-5 total)
  Cons: each write rewritten ~10x as it propagates levels
  Use: read-heavy, random reads (customer profile)

Time-Window (TWCS):
  Window 2024-10-01: [S_w1]   (one SSTable per window)
  Window 2024-10-02: [S_w2]
  Window 2024-10-03: [S_w3]
  ...
  TTL expires 2024-10-31 -> just delete S_w1 (file deletion)
  Pros: zero tombstone overhead, instant expiry
  Cons: only good for time-bucketed data with TTL
  Use: time-series with TTL (metrics, logs, sensor data)

Pick:
  write-heavy, infrequent reads       -> STCS
  read-heavy, frequently read         -> LCS
  time-series with TTL                -> TWCS
```

### Q7. What is the difference between SimpleStrategy and NetworkTopologyStrategy for replication?
**Answer:** **SimpleStrategy** places replicas sequentially clockwise on the ring starting from the partition's owner — it ignores rack/DC topology. You specify only `replication_factor: N`. It's suitable only for **single-DC dev/test clusters** because it doesn't survive rack failures (if replicas 1 and 2 happen to be in the same rack and that rack fails, you've lost 2 of 3 copies). **NetworkTopologyStrategy** (NTS) is rack/DC-aware — you specify RF per DC (e.g., `{'us-east': 3, 'us-west': 3, 'eu-west': 3}`). Within each DC, NTS places replicas on different racks when possible — if RF=3 in a DC with 3 racks, each replica goes on a different rack. This survives: **(a) Node failure** — replicas on other nodes. **(b) Rack failure** — replicas on other racks (loses a power strip or top-of-rack switch). **(c) DC failure** — replicas in other DCs (loses a whole region). NTS also supports **asymmetric replication** — you might want 3 replicas in your primary DC (for read throughput) but only 1 in a backup DC (just for disaster recovery). Real-world: Netflix runs 3 DCs (us-east-1, us-west-2, eu-west-1) with NTS RF=3 per DC = 9 total copies of each row. A whole DC can fail and they keep serving traffic from the other two. SimpleStrategy is essentially never used in production. **Rule**: if you have more than one rack or more than one DC, use NTS — even if RF=1 per DC, NTS will spread replicas across racks correctly.
**Visual:**
```
SimpleStrategy (RF=3):
  Ring: N1 -> N2 -> N3 -> N4 -> N5 -> N6
  Partition key hashes to N2's range.
  Replicas: N2, N3, N4  (next 2 clockwise)
  If N2, N3 in same rack and rack fails -> 2 of 3 copies LOST.

NetworkTopologyStrategy (RF=3 per DC, 3 racks each):

  DC: us-east-1 (racks R1, R2, R3)
    N1@R1, N2@R2, N3@R3
  DC: us-west-2 (racks R4, R5, R6)
    N4@R4, N5@R5, N6@R6

  Partition key hashes to N1's range.
  Replicas in us-east-1: N1@R1, N2@R2, N3@R3 (one per rack!)
  Replicas in us-west-2: N4@R4, N5@R5, N6@R6 (one per rack!)

  Survives:
    + any single node failure
    + any single rack failure (power, top-of-rack switch)
    + any single DC failure (entire region)
    + combination (one rack in DC1 + one rack in DC2)

Use NTS for any production cluster with >1 rack or >1 DC.
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You're building Instagram's home feed for 2B users. Each user follows up to 7500 accounts. How do you model this in Cassandra?
**Answer:** Use a **fan-out-on-write** model with the feed table keyed by `user_id`. Schema: `CREATE TABLE feed (user_id text, created_at timestamp, post_id uuid, author_id text, content text, PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), created_at, post_id)) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (created_at DESC, post_id ASC)`. When user Alice posts, a worker iterates her followers and inserts a row into each follower's feed partition — so reading a feed is a single-partition scan (`SELECT * FROM feed WHERE user_id=? LIMIT 50`), sub-10ms. For RF=3 and QUORUM writes, each post fan-out is durable. **Celebrity problem**: a user with 10M followers would trigger 10M writes per post — too slow. Fix with **hybrid fan-out**: for normal users (<100k followers), fan out on write; for celebrities (>=100k followers), don't fan out — instead, when a user reads their feed, merge their precomputed feed with the latest posts from celebrities they follow (a separate `celebrity_posts` table keyed by `author_id`, range-scanned by `created_at`). The cutoff depends on write throughput — Instagram uses ~100k followers. **Partition size limit**: each user's feed partition must stay under ~2 GB; with 50-byte rows and a 1000-post feed cap, that's ~50 KB per user — fine. For users with millions of followers, the fan-out cost dominates — they're handled by the hybrid path. Real-world: Instagram runs Cassandra on hundreds of nodes per DC, NTS RF=3 across 3+ DCs, with TWCS for time-based feed expiry (drop rows older than 30 days by TTL).
**Visual:**
```
Tables:
  feed (user_id, created_at, post_id, author_id, content)
    PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), created_at, post_id)
    -> read: SELECT * FROM feed WHERE user_id='alice' LIMIT 50

  celebrity_posts (author_id, created_at, post_id, content)
    PRIMARY KEY ((author_id), created_at, post_id)
    -> read: SELECT * FROM celebrity_posts
             WHERE author_id='kim_k' AND created_at > ?
             LIMIT 50

Write path (Alice posts, 1000 followers):
  fan-out worker:
    for follower in alice.followers:
      INSERT INTO feed (user_id, ...) VALUES (follower, ...)

Celebrity post (Kim K, 10M followers):
  do NOT fan out
  INSERT INTO celebrity_posts (author_id='kim_k', ...)

Read path (Bob's feed):
  1. SELECT * FROM feed WHERE user_id='bob' LIMIT 50
  2. For each celebrity Bob follows:
       SELECT * FROM celebrity_posts WHERE author_id=celeb
             AND created_at > bob.last_read
  3. Merge, sort by created_at, return top 50
```

### Q2. Netflix stores viewing history for 200M+ users in Cassandra. A new feature requires "show me users who watched X and Y" — a query Cassandra doesn't support natively. What do you do?
**Answer:** Cassandra's data model is **query-driven** — each table supports one access pattern efficiently. "Show me users who watched X and Y" is a **secondary index** query (filter on `movie_id`), which Cassandra supports via SASI (SSTable Attached Secondary Indexes) but performs poorly at scale (scatter-gather across all nodes). Three approaches: **(1) Build a dedicated table** for this query: `CREATE TABLE movie_watchers (movie_id text, user_id text, watched_at timestamp, PRIMARY KEY ((movie_id), user_id))` — populate it on every watch event (dual-write to the original `watch_history` table and this new one). Now `SELECT user_id FROM movie_watchers WHERE movie_id='X'` is a single-partition scan. To find users who watched X AND Y, query both movie partitions in parallel and intersect in the application layer. **(2) Use a search engine** (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch) for the analytical query — Cassandra stays the source of truth for transactional reads, and a CDC (Change Data Capture) stream populates Elasticsearch for ad-hoc queries. This is the standard pattern when query patterns evolve unpredictably. **(3) Use Spark + Cassandra** for batch analytics — Spark reads Cassandra partitions in parallel, does the join in memory, writes results to a summary table. Real-world: Netflix uses both — dedicated tables for known access patterns (e.g., "trending now" per region) and Elasticsearch for ad-hoc analytics. The rule: **don't make Cassandra do joins** — model each query as a table, or push complex queries to a system designed for them (Spark, ES, Presto).
**Visual:**
```
Original table (transactional):
  watch_history (user_id, watched_at, movie_id, ...)
    PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), watched_at, movie_id)
    -> query: "what did alice watch?" (fast)
    -> query: "who watched movie X?" (slow, scatter-gather)

Option 1: dedicated table for the new query
  movie_watchers (movie_id, user_id, watched_at)
    PRIMARY KEY ((movie_id), user_id)
    -> query: "who watched X?" -> single-partition scan (fast)
    -> query: "who watched X AND Y?" -> two parallel scans
                                     + intersect in app

  Cost: dual-write on every watch event (2x write throughput)
  Pro: fast, native Cassandra

Option 2: Cassandra + Elasticsearch
  Cassandra: source of truth, transactional reads
  CDC stream (e.g., Debezium) -> Elasticsearch index
  ES query: "movie_id:X AND movie_id:Y" (native for ES)
  Pro: supports ANY future query
  Con: new system to operate, eventual consistency window

Option 3: Spark batch job
  Nightly job reads watch_history in parallel
  Computes "users who watched X and Y"
  Writes results to a summary table in Cassandra
  Pro: handles complex analytics
  Con: not real-time (hours latency)

Pick: option 1 if it's a known, stable query.
      option 2 if query patterns evolve.
      option 3 for batch analytics.
```

### Q3. Your Cassandra cluster's reads just got 5× slower after a traffic spike. The ops dashboard shows many SSTables per shard. Diagnose and fix.
**Answer:** The slowdown is likely **read amplification from too many uncompacted SSTables**. Diagnose with `nodetool compactionstats` (shows pending compactions) and `nodetool tablestats` (shows `Space used (live)` and `Number of partitions (live)` per table; high SSTable count per partition is the smoking gun). Also `nodetool cfstats <keyspace>.<table>` shows `SSTable count` — if it's >15 per partition, reads are doing too many disk I/Os. Common causes and fixes: **(1) Compaction fell behind** — if writes exceed compaction throughput, SSTables pile up. Fix: increase `compaction_throughput_mb_per_sec` (default 16; raise to 64-128 during catch-up), or temporarily disable writes to the affected table. **(2) Wrong compaction strategy** — STCS on a read-heavy table means many SSTables per read. Switch to LCS via `ALTER TABLE ... WITH compaction = {'class': 'LeveledCompactionStrategy'}`. **(3) Tombstone buildup** — if your workload writes and deletes rapidly (e.g., a queue), tombstones accumulate and reads scan them. Run `nodetool compactionstats` to see if tombstone compactions are pending; check `tombstone_warn_threshold` (default 1000 rows scanned). Fix: switch to a queue-appropriate system (Kafka), or use TTLs (which generate tombstones that compaction removes cleanly) instead of explicit deletes. **(4) Read-heavy workload outgrew STCS** — switch to LCS. **(5) Bloom filter false positives** — if `bloom_filter_fp_chance` is too high (default 0.01 for STCS, 0.1 for LCS), more SSTables are read per query; lower it. Real-world: a Netflix team hit this when shifting from write-heavy (viewing history) to read-heavy (recommendation features); switching the affected table from STCS to LCS cut p99 read latency from 80ms to 12ms.
**Visual:**
```
Diagnosis flowchart:

  Symptom: reads 5x slower after traffic spike
    |
    v
  nodetool compactionstats
    -> "pending compactions: 500" (high)
    -> compaction fell behind writes
    Fix: raise compaction_throughput_mb_per_sec to 64-128
         (or temporarily shed write load)

  nodetool tablestats keyspace.table
    -> "SSTable count: 25 per partition" (high, should be <5)
    -> read amplification
    Fix: switch STCS -> LCS for read-heavy table

  Check tombstones:
    -> "Tombstones scanned: 5000 per read" (high)
    -> tombstone buildup (writes+deletes pattern)
    Fix: use TTL instead of explicit DELETE
         or move queue-like workload to Kafka

  Check bloom filter:
    -> bloom_filter_fp_chance = 0.1 (high for LCS)
    -> many SSTables read per query unnecessarily
    Fix: ALTER TABLE ... bloom_filter_fp_chance = 0.01

  Monitoring:
    - read latency p99 (alert if > 50ms)
    - SSTable count per partition (alert if > 10)
    - tombstones scanned per read (alert if > 1000)
    - pending compactions (alert if > 100)
```

### Q4. Apple runs a 75,000-node Cassandra cluster for iMessage. How do they handle operations at that scale?
**Answer:** At 75k nodes, several things break that work fine at 100-node scale: **(1) Gossip traffic** — every node gossips to 1-3 peers per second; at 75k nodes, the gossip state itself is large (every node knows about every other). Apple splits the cluster into multiple **smaller rings** (often called "cell-based architecture") of ~1000-5000 nodes each, with cross-cell replication for HA. Each cell is operationally independent. **(2) Bootstrapping** — adding a node streams data from neighbors; at 75k nodes, a single bootstrap might stream terabytes. Apple pre-splits token ranges and uses **virtual node (vnode) tokens** (256 per node) so a new node takes small ranges from many existing nodes, parallelizing the stream. **(3) Schema changes** — `ALTER TABLE` propagates via gossip to all nodes; at 75k nodes, schema agreement can take minutes. Apple batches schema changes during low-traffic windows and uses `nodetool describecluster` to verify agreement before depending on the new schema. **(4) Compaction** — at this scale, compaction I/O can saturate disks. Apple uses dedicated compaction nodes (rare) or carefully tuned `compaction_throughput_mb_per_sec` to keep compaction from impacting foreground reads. **(5) Failure domain** — at 75k nodes, multiple nodes are always failing. Apple relies on NTS RF=3+ across multiple DCs; hinted handoff and read repair keep replicas consistent. **(6) Operations automation** — at this scale, manual ops are impossible. Apple uses Chef/Puppet/Ansible for provisioning, custom monitoring (Prometheus + Grafana with Cassandra exporters), and automated remediation (auto-replace dead nodes). The key insight: **don't build one giant ring** — build many smaller rings (cells) with cross-cell replication. Real-world: Apple, Netflix, and Spotify all use cell-based architecture for their largest Cassandra deployments.
**Visual:**
```
Cell-based architecture (Apple's iMessage):

  Cell 1 (us-east, 3000 nodes)
    - handles ~5% of users (shard by user_id hash)
    - ring: gossip within cell only
    - RF=3 within cell + cross-cell replication to Cell 2
    - independent schema, ops, deployments

  Cell 2 (us-east, 3000 nodes)
    - handles next 5% of users
    - ring: gossip within cell
    - cross-cell replication from Cell 1, to Cell 3
    ...

  Cell 25 (eu-west, 3000 nodes)
    - handles EU users
    ...

  Total: 25 cells * 3000 nodes = 75,000 nodes
  Each cell: operationally independent
  Cross-cell: async replication for disaster recovery

Why cells:
  + gossip stays O(cell_size) not O(cluster_size)
  + bootstrapping streams from local neighbors (fast)
  + schema agreement within cell only (fast)
  + failure in one cell doesn't affect others
  + canary deployments per cell
  - cross-cell replication adds complexity
  - some queries span cells (rare; design avoids)

Operations automation:
  - auto-replace dead nodes (Chef recipe)
  - Prometheus + Cassandra exporter monitoring
  - alerting: pending compactions, hint count, read latency
  - automated backups to S3 per cell
```

### Q5. You need to implement an atomic counter (e.g., "likes" on a post) in Cassandra. Standard updates aren't atomic. How?
**Answer:** Cassandra provides **counters** as a special data type — `UPDATE likes SET count = count + 1 WHERE post_id = ?` is atomic at the partition level. Under the hood, Cassandra uses a different write path for counters: each replica maintains its own counter shard (a local delta), and reads aggregate across replicas. Trade-offs: **(1) Counter updates are not idempotent** — replaying a counter increment (e.g., from a retry or hint replay) double-counts. Cassandra tracks which coordinator wrote each delta to mitigate this, but edge cases (coordinator crashes between ack and replay) can still over-count. **(2) Counters must be in their own table** — a counter column can't coexist with regular columns being updated (you can't `UPDATE posts SET likes = likes + 1, title = 'new' WHERE ...`). **(3) Counter reads are slower** — they aggregate across replicas rather than reading one. **(4) Counters don't work with lightweight transactions (Paxos)**. For high-throughput counters (millions of likes/sec on a viral post), the better pattern is **approximate counting**: maintain per-shard local counters in memory (e.g., per coordinator, per 5-minute window), flush to Cassandra periodically, and sum on read. This sacrifices exact accuracy (you might over/under-count by 0.1%) but eliminates the contention. Real-world: Twitter uses HyperLogLog for unique-viewer counts; Reddit uses sharded counters (one counter per `post_id + shard_id`, sum on read). For exact counting at low throughput, Cassandra counters work fine. For high throughput, sharded approximate counting is the answer.
**Visual:**
```
Cassandra counter (exact, low-throughput):

  CREATE TABLE post_likes (
    post_id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
    count   counter
  );

  UPDATE post_likes SET count = count + 1 WHERE post_id = ?;
  -> atomic at partition level
  -> each replica maintains its own delta
  -> read aggregates: SELECT count FROM post_likes WHERE post_id=?;
                          -> sum of all replica deltas

  Cons: not idempotent (retries double-count)
        must be in own table
        slower reads
        doesn't work with lightweight transactions

Sharded counters (approximate, high-throughput):

  CREATE TABLE post_likes_sharded (
    post_id    uuid,
    shard_id   int,
    count      counter,
    PRIMARY KEY ((post_id), shard_id)
  );

  Write path (per coordinator):
    shard = hash(coordinator_id + minute) % 64
    UPDATE post_likes_sharded SET count = count + 1
      WHERE post_id = ? AND shard_id = ?;

  Read path:
    SELECT count FROM post_likes_sharded WHERE post_id = ?;
    -> sum all 64 shards in app

  Pros: writes spread across 64 shards (no hotspot)
        retries still double-count but per-shard (manageable)
  Cons: 64x storage, sum-on-read latency

Real-world: Twitter (HyperLogLog for uniques),
            Reddit (64-shard counters for upvotes)
```

### Q6. A node in your Cassandra cluster has been down for 4 hours. It just came back. What happens, and what do you need to check?
**Answer:** When the node comes back online: **(1) Gossip marks it UP** — within ~10 seconds, peers detect the node responding to gossip and update their state. **(2) Hinted handoff begins** — coordinators that stashed writes for the down node start replaying them. If hints are large (4 hours of writes), this can take hours and saturate the node's I/O. **(3) Read repair kicks in** — for reads touching this node, the coordinator notices stale data and writes the latest back (async read repair). **(4) The node rejoins the ring** and starts serving traffic. **Things to check**: **(a) Hint backlog** — `nodetool tpstats` shows `HintBacklog` in the hints service; if it's huge (>1M), consider disabling hinted handoff (`nodetool disablehintsfordc` temporarily) and running `nodetool repair` instead, which is more controlled. **(b) Compaction backlog** — the node missed 4 hours of compactions; SSTables have piled up. Run `nodetool compactionstats` and let compaction catch up before declaring the node healthy. **(c) Data staleness** — run `nodetool repair -pr <keyspace>` (parallel repair, partitioner range) to ensure the node is fully consistent with replicas. **(d) Read latency** — the node will be slow for a while (cold cache, hint replay competing for I/O); consider keeping it out of the read pool (`nodetool drain` then restart with reduced read load). **(e) Hint directory disk usage** — `du -sh /var/lib/cassandra/hints` on each coordinator; if it's gigabytes, the replay will take a while. **(f) Tune `max_hint_window_in_ms`** (default 3 hours) — if a node is down longer than this, hints are dropped; you MUST run `nodetool repair` after recovery. For a 4-hour outage, you've lost 1 hour of hints — repair is mandatory. Real-world: Netflix runs `nodetool repair -pr` weekly on all keyspaces as a defensive measure against silent staleness.
**Visual:**
```
Node recovery timeline:

  T=0     node N3 dies (host crash)
  T=0..4h coordinators stash hints for N3 (up to max_hint_window=3h)
          After 3h, hints are DROPPED (silent data loss on N3's view)
  T=4h    N3 recovers, starts gossip
  T=4h+10s peers mark N3 UP
  T=4h+1m hinted handoff begins (replay 3h of stashed hints)
          -> I/O saturated, N3 slow to serve reads
  T=4h+30m hints replayed (3h of writes, takes 30min to replay)
          -> N3 has last 3h of data, missing the 1h before that
  T=4h+30m run `nodetool repair -pr <keyspace>` (mandatory)
          -> streams missing data from peers
          -> takes another 30min-2h depending on data size
  T=4h+2h  N3 fully consistent, healthy
          -> compaction catches up on backlog
          -> read latency returns to normal

Monitoring during recovery:
  + nodetool tpstats (HintBacklog should decrease to 0)
  + nodetool compactionstats (pending compactions)
  + nodetool netstats (streaming progress)
  + read latency p99 (will be elevated during recovery)

Preventive measures:
  + raise max_hint_window_in_ms to 1 day (costs disk space)
  + schedule weekly `nodetool repair -pr` for all keyspaces
  + monitor hint directory size on each coordinator
  + alert on any node down > 1 hour (run repair after recovery)
```

### Q7. You're designing a multi-region Cassandra deployment for a global e-commerce site. Each region should serve its local users with low latency, but all regions must see consistent inventory counts. How?
**Answer:** The fundamental tension: multi-region writes are slow to synchronize (cross-region latency 50-150ms), but inventory needs strong consistency (can't oversell). Two patterns: **(1) Last-write-wins (LWW) with quorum reads** — use `EACH_QUORUM` writes (quorum in every DC) and `QUORUM` reads. With RF=3 in each of 3 DCs (9 total copies), EACH_QUORUM waits for 2 of 3 in each DC = 6 acks, with cross-region latency. This gives strong consistency but high write latency (~150ms). Suitable for low-write, critical data (inventory, account balances). **(2) Single-DC writes + async replication** — writes go to one DC (e.g., us-east), Cassandra replicates to other DCs asynchronously. Reads in other DCs may be stale (eventually consistent). For inventory, this risks overselling if two regions read the same "1 item left" simultaneously. Pattern (1) is right for inventory; pattern (2) is right for user profiles (eventually consistent is fine). For inventory specifically: **model as a counter table** with `EACH_QUORUM` writes — `UPDATE inventory SET count = count - 1 WHERE sku = ?` is atomic and strong. Better still, **don't share inventory across regions** — pre-allocate stock per region (us-east has 1000 of SKU X, eu-west has 500). This eliminates cross-region coordination entirely; each region's inventory is local-only. For global stock visibility (e.g., "show me total inventory"), maintain a separate analytics table updated by Spark batch. Real-world: Amazon pre-allocates inventory per fulfillment center; cross-FC transfers are explicit operations, not real-time. The lesson: **don't use strong cross-region consistency unless absolutely necessary** — restructure the data model to localize consistency requirements.
**Visual:**
```
Option A: EACH_QUORUM (strong, slow):

  us-east (RF=3)    us-west (RF=3)    eu-west (RF=3)
    N1,N2,N3         N4,N5,N6          N7,N8,N9

  Write inventory sku=X, count=99 (EACH_QUORUM):
    coordinator sends to all 9 nodes
    waits for QUORUM in EACH DC (2 of 3 per DC = 6 acks)
    cross-region latency: ~150ms
  Read (QUORUM):
    reads from any DC's quorum
    -> strong consistency guaranteed

  Pro: strong consistency globally
  Con: 150ms write latency (unacceptable for high-QPS writes)

Option B: pre-allocate inventory per region:

  inventory table:
    PRIMARY KEY ((region, sku), ...)
    rows: (us-east, X, 1000)   <- only us-east can decrement
            (us-west, X, 500)
            (eu-west, X, 800)

  Each region writes only to its own partition:
    UPDATE inventory SET count = count - 1
      WHERE region='us-east' AND sku='X';
    -> LOCAL_QUORUM in us-east (fast, ~10ms)
    -> no cross-region coordination

  Cross-region transfers (rare, manual):
    Begin batch:
      UPDATE inventory SET count = count - 100
        WHERE region='us-east' AND sku='X';
      UPDATE inventory SET count = count + 100
        WHERE region='us-west' AND sku='X';
    Apply batch (coordinated by app-level saga)

  Global visibility (analytics):
    Materialized view or Spark job:
      SELECT region, sku, count FROM inventory;
      -> sum per sku across regions

  Pro: fast local writes, no cross-region latency
  Con: requires pre-allocation logic, transfer operations
  Use: e-commerce inventory, ride-sharing driver allocation
```
